So first off, I wasn't talking about annual veggies. I was talking about perennials that had overwintered in the ground. The confusion was my fault, for posting while I was in a complete daze after seeing the damage. I do have a couple of transplants, but nothing I was too worried about losing.

Overall, things aren't as dire as I originally thought. Don't get me wrong, I've got some hellacious damage, but I think I can salvage something from most everything.

I went outside about 2am to check on the plants and animals. I'd been tossing and turning having nightmares of the wind tearing my greenhouse down and killing all my starts. Everything was covered with frozen rain, and the soil was frozen about an inch deep. The crusty kind of frozen, not the can't dig in it frozen. Went back in and turned on the TV before eventually falling back asleep to the voice of Mike Aston talking about a Roman bridge.

Come morning and my worst fears were true. Everything was frozen through. I could snap last years growth off my fruit trees with two fingers, my daffodils would shatter when I broke them off and dropped them, and everything had that dark dark green color of severe damage. If I touched a leaf, it would fall and crack.

Now that I'm home and the weather is in the 40s, I'm actually surprised at how much isn't completely flat from being frozen. My hyacinth is all killed down to the mulch, but my tulips are happy as could be. My brocolli, cabbage, and cauliflower, the only transplants, are pretty shot, but the tiny in-situ sown seedlings of them a row over are fine. My herbaceous herbs like valerian and lovage are fucked.

My more expensive plants though, epimediums, astilbes, brunneras, etc, took a hard hit. I honestly don't know if my epimediums are going to make it. Thats hard hit for me. Unsurprisingly, the edelweisse is fine, and most of the other alpine flowers.

My trees I'm not sure about. I'm definitely not getting any fruit this year from them. Maybe the pears, as they just started to bud. I'm mostly worried about damage to the trunks. As long as I've got a solid trunk I can top them and graft new wood, but I think I'm going to get some significant damage regardless.

Onbig thing I've learned is that the plants under the trees, even the dormant trees, did much better than those open to the sky. I think I've going to have to hold off on expanding beyond the limits of those trees until the saplings get large enough to provide cover and wind protection. The wind is what really did it. The temps didn't officially get below 26, but the gale force winds ripping through my valley were devastating to anything exposed to its chill.

So overall, I guess I won't burn down my house and move back to Texas. I'll wait a few years until it does this again and then pot up what I want to take with me before burning it down...
An assessment of my freeze damage from last night.
